metadata.title: What are Creative Commons Licenses?
metadata.description:
This work is licensed under a Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-ShareAlike 4.0 International License https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc-sa/4.0/

Transcript:
This video will introduce you to Creative Commons licenses, which makes copyright easier to understand.

Let’s say you create something. 

This thing could be creative, like a picture of your cat, or scholarly, like an essay about cats.

Because you are the creator of this picture or this essay, copyright allows you to decide what people can do with your creation.

[Dialogue bubble appears on screen: X is okay but you shouldn’t do Y with my work.]

When you are the copyright holder, people have to ask you for permission before putting your cat picture into a PowerPoint or adapting your cat essay into a movie. 

Getting permission can be time consuming and complicated for both the creator and the user.

[The following dialogue bubbles appear on screen: Who has copyright? How do I contact them?! I need to know if I can use this ASAP (as soon as possible)!]

This is where Creative Commons can help. 

Creative Commons exists to make permissions explicit and straightforward.

Creative Commons licenses use icons and simple language so that creators can make their intentions clear and users can be certain that their use of a work is legal. 

[Sample Creative Commons license displayed. The Attribution-ShareAlike 3.0 Unported license has icons above the title. Below the title is the simple language section detailing what “You are free to” do in terms of sharing and adapting under this license]

These different licenses help people understand if and how they can use, share, or build on a work.

[The six different Creative Common licenses are displayed on screen]

This icon [Noncommercial] means that only non-commercial uses are permitted, so no one can profit from using your picture.

[Noncommercial icon has a dollar sign with a circle around it and a slash through it]

This icon [No Derivatives] means that no one can make changes to the original work, such as photoshopping a dog into your cat picture.

[No Derivatives icon is an equal sign with a circle around it]

This icon [Share Alike] means that someone can change your work, but their version must be shared under the same license as yours.

[Share Alike icon is a circle with an opening on the left side, the top side of the opening has an arrow pointing down to the where the circle begins again]

All Creative Commons licenses give credit to the original creator, preserving your reputation as a creative genius while the world engages with your work.

[Creative Commons license is displayed on screen with emphasis on the By icon (which is a the silhouette of a person with a circle around it)]

Licenses can be attached to most things, including blog posts, images, artworks, journal articles, and more! 

To learn more about Creative Commons licenses, visit the Creative Commons website or check out some of the other videos in our series.

metadata.title: Socrate | Il filosofo che non scrisse nulla
metadata.description:
Socrate non ha scritto una sola riga, eppure ha cambiato per sempre la filosofia.
Chi era davvero l'uomo che Platone trasformò nel simbolo stesso del filosofo?
Una lezione sul significato profondo della filosofia, tra ironia, dialogo e ricerca della verità.

Che cosa immaginiamo quando sentiamo la parola "filosofo"? Un professore universitario? Un autore di libri difficili? Un intellettuale chiuso nel proprio studio?
Per i Greci la risposta sarebbe stata molto diversa.
Con Socrate nasce infatti un modo completamente nuovo di intendere la filosofia: non come accumulo di conoscenze, ma come esercizio quotidiano dell'esistenza. Socrate non scrisse nulla, eppure tutta la filosofia occidentale si è sviluppata a partire dalla sua figura. Platone, Senofonte, Aristofane e molti altri ci hanno lasciato immagini diverse, talvolta opposte, di un uomo destinato a diventare il simbolo stesso della ricerca della verità.
Nel corso della lezione analizzeremo il rapporto fra Socrate e i Sofisti, il significato dell'ironia, della maieutica e della brachilogia, il celebre "sapere di non sapere", il legame con il motto delfico "Conosci te stesso" e il ruolo educativo del dialogo. Scopriremo inoltre perché Aristotele considera Socrate l'inventore del concetto e come, da lui, abbiano preso origine quasi tutte le grandi scuole filosofiche dell'antichità.
Una riflessione che conduce inevitabilmente anche a una domanda molto attuale: quale dovrebbe essere oggi il compito di un vero insegnante?

metadata.title: Your BRAIN is LYING to YOU
metadata.description:
What if everything you remember isn't actually real? A neuroscientist explains how your brain constantly confabulates and deceives you about reality itself.

0:00 The Confabulous Brain Intro
1:03 Philosophy of Reality & The Matrix
4:18 Mrs. B's Case of Confabulation
6:46 Brain Damage & Confabulation Syndrome
8:11 True vs False Memory in the Brain
9:32 Study on Reality Recognition
12:34 Prefrontal Cortex & Fantasy vs Reality
14:00 Electrical Signals & Belief

Ever wonder if your memories are accurate or if your brain is playing tricks on you? In this eye-opening talk, neuroscientist Matthew Collins explores the fascinating concept of the "confabulous brain"—how our minds constantly construct false memories and distort reality without us even knowing it. Drawing parallels to The Matrix and classical philosophy from Descartes, Collins reveals the unsettling truth: you can't always trust your own senses or memories. If you can't tell the difference between what's real and what your brain imagined, how do you know anything is real at all? This talk challenges everything you think you know about consciousness, perception, and the nature of reality itself.

#neuroscience #psychology #memory #consciousness #brain #philosophy #reality #tedx

metadata.description:
Welcome to FreeRise. 

What If everything we experience through our five senses is only a tiny fraction of Reality?

In this fascinating conversation with Arun, we go beyond signs, synchronicities and extraordinary experiences to explore a much bigger question: Are there other dimensions of life and reality that we simply cannot perceive?

Could there be aspects of existence beyond the physical world? Is consciousness limited to our brain and five senses? And could some of the experiences we dismiss as coincidence, intuition or imagination actually be glimpses of something we don't yet fully understand?

This conversation takes us into the fascinating world of other dimensions, consciousness, reality, intuition, synchronicities and the unseen aspects of existence.

FROM SIGNS… TO WHAT LIES BEYOND

What exactly are "Other Dimensions"?

When we hear the word "dimension," we often think of science fiction or something mysterious and impossible to understand.
But what if the idea is far more interesting than that?
We begin by looking at the dimensions we experience in everyday life - length, breadth and height - and the fourth dimension, time.
From there, we explore the possibility of realities beyond the physical dimensions we normally experience.

Our conversation touches on questions such as:
• What do we actually mean when we talk about "other dimensions"?
• Could human beings already have experiences connected to realities beyond the physical world?
• Could intuition, déjà vu, dreams, synchronicities or unexplained experiences be clues to something we don't yet understand?
• Why can't we perceive these dimensions through our normal senses?
• Is consciousness something more than the physical activity of the brain?
• Could our five senses be limiting our understanding of reality?
• Why do some experiences feel as though they transcend ordinary explanations?
• And perhaps most importantly—what if the reality we know is only part of a much bigger picture?

This is not a conversation intended to tell you what to believe.
It is an invitation to question, explore and stay curious.

A CONVERSATION, NOT A CONCLUSION

Some of the ideas discussed in this episode may resonate deeply with you. Others may make you skeptical.
That's perfectly fine.

The purpose of these conversations is not to prove that one particular explanation is correct. It is to explore questions that sit at the intersection of consciousness, spirituality, human experience and our understanding of reality.
Sometimes the most interesting questions are the ones for which we don't yet have all the answers.

metadata.description:
Fall asleep to the story of the young Nietzsche, who worshipped Schopenhauer and spent his life trying to prove him wrong.

As a lonely student, Friedrich Nietzsche found a dead philosopher's book on a bookshop table and fell under a spell that would shape everything he became. This episode follows the long, strange bond between Nietzsche and his first master, Arthur Schopenhauer, from devotion to open war. We meet the bitter, solitary Schopenhauer and his vision of a blind striving world where life is suffering and the wisest thing is to want less. We watch the young Nietzsche pour that vision into his first book, then slowly turn against it, until he answers the darkest case ever made against existence with the wildest possible affirmation of it. Along the way we trace the will, pity, the death of the hidden true world, and the thought that measures whether a life could be loved enough to live again. It is a quiet, patient walk through the deepest argument two honest minds ever had about whether life is worth wanting.

Please listen only in safe, restful contexts.

There are times when the world seems to be changing faster than our understanding of it.

Old assumptions are questioned. Familiar structures begin to feel less certain. And many people find themselves asking what comes next.

In this episode of Between Realms and Reason, Heather Ensworth explores the possibility that periods of uncertainty and disruption can also be periods of profound transformation.

The conversation moves beyond astrology into questions about consciousness, healing, intuition, relationship, and what humanity may be learning as old paradigms begin to shift.

In this episode, you'll explore:
• ancient cosmic cycles and their relationship to human consciousness
• the Age of Aquarius
• the Kali Yuga and humanity's experience of forgetting
• trauma, healing, and separation
• intuition and expanded awareness
• the relationship between individual and collective transformation
• why old ways of understanding may no longer feel sufficient
• what remembering might mean for humanity's future

Whether you approach these ideas spiritually, symbolically, psychologically, or simply with curiosity, this conversation invites you to consider a larger question:
What if transformation isn't only about creating something new—but remembering something we've forgotten?
